Hi HN, I am a facial cosmetic surgeon and have been practicing for just over 20 years. I work in Beverly Hills and Miami and my practice is both surgical and non-surgical (ie fillers) and I specialize in very natural results.

I always tell patients: the procedures are easy to do but making it look natural is the hard part. I am constantly surprised at the interactions I have with patients who don't have the experience to know when another provider is selling them on treatments that I know either don't work or can even cause harm long-term. I also realize I can only serve 1 patient at a time.

I wanted to try democratize the consultation experience and give patients the information needed to make an informed decision based upon the published literature and my own clinical experience.

The website I created is called MyMirrorMD.com and is designed to help patients know what treatments would be supported for their unique face, in what volumes/amount and approximate price points. I've also added a section called "guide" that compares common treatments and answers many of the questions I have fielded day after day for many years.

Would love to know your feedback on this project, which is my first foray into using AI and building a website!

latest.text:
I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline.

The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04.

Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD.

To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge.

Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback":

1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge.

2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk.

3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now.

The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform.

As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable.

If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem.

Pura vida!

R.S.G.

latest.text:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

Hi HN!

Fakeipedia is an automatic world-building platform which takes an imagined world and makes a whole wiki that you can endlessly explore by clicking red links.

I came up with this idea a few months ago after playing around with worldbuilding in Gemini, but I didn't want to release it until a powerful enough model could do it justice, and I decided that Argon is creative enough to write articles that are worth reading. I was surprised how well it turned out and how engaging some of the writing actually is.

If you want to generate an article there is a nominal charge attached ($0.90), which helps cover AI/Stripe costs, and I think I just about break even. You can also steer the generation ala choose-your-own-adventure books when generating a new article. Everything generated is free and public for everyone to see.

I hope you like it and I'm very much open to hearing about new world ideas/features that would make this project better.

I've been building a bunch of consumer apps lately around personalization and recommendation and have had a hard time finding this data in one spot. agents can find useful stuff through tool calls / web search, but slow.

you can scrape on demand too, but i wanted a faster data set and couldn't find an existing provider for the mix of event types I was searching for.

the methodology for it is to find influential accounts/posters/etc. and do a fan out across things that they co-post with.

mcp: `claude mcp add --transport http thingstodo https://api.thingstodoapi.com/mcp`

I'm considering adding other cities. If you're building something that needs local event data, would something like this be useful and where would you want coverage?

Hi HN,

I’ve been working on esp32sim, an open-source ESP32 emulator that runs in the browser.

The fun part of the demo is that there is no ESP32 involved — the firmware is executing in the emulator.

The goal is to make ESP32 software easier to experiment with, test and simulate without always needing physical hardware connected.

Source: https://github.com/mikroverk/esp32sim

I made a short video showing it in action: https://youtu.be/waoWFilTWEc

I’m particularly interested in feedback from embedded developers: what would an emulator like this need to support before you’d actually use it for development, testing or CI?
